Title: A sparse and invisible targeted backdoor attack in federated learning

A sparse and invisible targeted backdoor attack in federated learning

Abstract
In distributed edge Computing scenarios within the Internet of Things (IoT), individual clients are susceptible to adversarial
backdoor attacks, wherein malicious modiﬁcations to local data may be introduced. Such compromised clients can negatively
impact the integrity and performance of the global model during federated learning. Existing backdoor attack techniques
suffer from low attack success rates and poor trigger concealment. To address this issue, this paper proposes a novel Sparse
and Invisible Targeted Backdoor (SITB) attack method. The key advantages of SITB are as follows: (1) A sparse and invisible
trigger generation approach is introduced, enforcing sparsity and invisibility constraints during optimization to enhance trigger
concealment. (2) In sparse constraints, by ranking gradient values and selecting pixels most sensitive to the model, the method
achieves a high attack success rate. Extensive experiments on the CIFAR-10 public dataset and PathMNIST dataset validate the
effectiveness of the proposed method. Results show that the attack success rate on poisoned data surpasses existing methods
by 5–10%. Furthermore, the quantitative assessment of visual quality, conducted both prior to and subsequent to poisoning,
afﬁrmed that the generated trigger exhibited a high degree of stealthiness, boasting a PSNR value as high as 40 and an SSIM
value as high as 0.99. In addition, SPAM and SRM are extremely low. Moreover, it demonstrates robust resistance against
multiple federated learning defense mechanisms.
Keywords Internet of things · Federated learning · Backdoor attack · Invisibility · Security
1 Introduction
Federated learning (FL) has emerged as a pivotal tech-
nology for privacy-preserving distributed machine learning,
particularly in Internet of Things (IoT) ecosystems, where
edge devices—such as sensors, smartphones, and industrial
controllers—collaboratively train models without sharing
raw data (Chen et al. 2023). It effectively mitigates the data
silo problem while ensuring the security of each partici-
pant’s data (Zhang et al. 2021). However, federated learning’s

injecting triggers into the training data and modifying labels
to target labels, attackers cause the model to learn the associ-
ation between the triggers and the target labels. The poisoned
local models are then uploaded to the server, contaminating
the aggregated global model. Consequently, during the pre-
diction phase, when the attacker inputs data containing the
triggers, the model incorrectly outputs the attacker-speciﬁed
target label (Bagdasaryan et al. 2020; Wang et al. 2020).
Therefore, trigger design plays a pivotal role in the effective-
ness of backdoor attacks.
Various methods have been proposed for generating trig-
gers (Gong et al. 2023; Cheng et al. 2021). Patch-based
triggers (Li et al. 2020) and additive triggers (Barni et al.
2019; Li et al. 2021) are widely used. Patch-based triggers
are sparse, affecting only a few pixels, but the added pertur-
bations are often visible to the human eye and can be detected

Overall, designing a backdoor trigger that is both sparse and

This paper focuses on trigger generation methods. Unlike
other triggers, the proposed trigger achieves both high attack
success rates and strong concealment. In federated learn-
ing, the large number of participating clients, the diversity
of client data, and the random selection of clients for train-
ing in each round may dilute the poisoning effect of malicious
clients over time. However, the proposed poisoning method
demonstrates outstanding performance. The poisoned data
from malicious clients is effectively learned by the model and
continues to inﬂuence subsequent training until the model
converges normally, maintaining a high attack success rate.
In summary, this paper makes the following key contribu-
tions:
1. A sparse and invisible trigger generation method is pro-
posed, enforcing both sparsity and invisibility during the
generation process to enhance concealment.
2. When enforcing the sparsity of the trigger, a gradient-
based optimization algorithm is used to select model-
sensitive pixels as poisoned pixels, achieving a high
attack success rate.
3. Experimental results show that the proposed trigger
achieves a 5-10% higher attack success rate and a 4-10
increase in peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) compared
to existing methods. In addition, SPAM and SRM are
extremely low. Additionally, SITB effectively resists
multiple federated learning defense mechanisms.

2 Related work
2.1 Backdoor attack
In federated learning, the objective of a backdoor attack is to
manipulate the global model such that it outputs a speciﬁc
prediction label for certain input data containing predeﬁned
perturbations. Once the model converges, the attacker can
input data with these perturbations to obtain the desired target
label. The goal is to ensure that all samples with the speciﬁc
perturbation are classiﬁed as the target label rather than their
original labels (Liu et al. 2024). Backdoor attacks typically
involve adding speciﬁc perturbations, known as triggers, to
the training data, causing the model to output the target label
when it detects these perturbations. Therefore, trigger design
is central to backdoor attacks in federated learning. Recent
studies classify trigger design into two main categories: addi-
tive triggers and patch-based triggers.
Bad-Nets is a representative patch-based trigger gener-
ation method. It introduces a ﬁxed pattern as a patch to
images, modifying the label to the target class. This method
is simple and easy to implement but is highly detectable by
manual inspection. Li et al. (2020) improved this approach
by adjusting the transparency of the trigger, making it less
perceptible to human eyes. Subsequently, Li et al. (2019)
extended backdoor attacks to physical environments, demon-
strating potential risks in real-world applications. Recently,
Li et al. (2022) introduced a targetless backdoor attack using
patch-based triggers, combining invisibility and harmless-
ness while providing a mechanism for verifying copyright
ownership.Mostexistingstudiesdefaulttousingpatch-based
triggers due to their clear sparsity and ease of implemen-
tation. These methods allow rapid generation of poisoned
data through a patching approach and can pose threats even
in physical environments (Li et al. 2020, 2022). However,
researchers often limit the size, number, and transparency of
the triggers to achieve invisibility, yet the perturbation effects
remain noticeable.
In recent years, additive triggers have also gained atten-
tion. For example, Zhao et al. (2020) implemented clean-
label backdoor attacks, avoiding detection caused by label
anomalies and introducing new security challenges in video
recognition tasks. Li et al. (2021) designed a new attack
paradigm in which each poisoned sample has a unique trig-
ger instead of using a uniform trigger. Moreover, the trigger
is implemented by embedding an imperceptible perturba-
tion into the image, effectively bypassing existing backdoor
detection mechanisms. Yang et al. (2023) combined sparse
perturbations, set distortions, and adversarial noise to gen-
erate efﬁcient backdoor attacks. Li et al. (2021) generated
hidden triggers for speciﬁc samples, enabling highly efﬁ-
cient and hard-to-detect attacks. Zhang et al. (2024) proposed
A3FL, which adaptively adjusts backdoor triggers to enhance
attack persistence during global training dynamics. By gen-
erating unique triggers for each poisoned sample, they
signiﬁcantly improved concealment and ﬂexibility.
Overall, additive triggers perform better in terms of invis-
ibility because attackers can limit the perturbation range.
However, these methods modify nearly all pixels, lacking
sparsity and reducing feasibility in real-world applications.
They also exhibit low attack success rates and poor conceal-
ment. To adapt to stronger backdoor detection technologies
and promote federated learning robustness, there is an urgent

2.2 FL defense
Federated learning defense techniques have evolved from
robust aggregation to anomaly detection, each with its own
advantages and limitations for different attack scenarios.
Early methods like Krum, a Byzantine aggregation rule,
calculate the similarity between client gradients and select
updates closest to the normal distribution. However, its effec-
tiveness diminishes with many malicious clients. Trimmed
Mean sorts client updates, discards extreme values, and
aggregates the remaining updates. This method requires
accurate estimation of the proportion of malicious clients.
With the widespread deployment of federated learning
in distributed scenarios such as vehicular ad hoc networks
(VANETs) and 5G edge computing, its security and com-
munication trustworthiness face multiple challenges. Al-
Shareeda et al. proposed an authentication mechanism based
on Chebyshev polynomials (Al-Shareeda et al. 2025), which
provides rapid response and node identity veriﬁcation for fog
computing environments without incurring high computa-
tional overhead, effectively preventing unauthorized devices
from impersonating legitimate ones. Subsequent research
further explored identity privacy and conditional revocabil-
ity, introducing identity-based cryptography (IBC) schemes
for privacy preservation in VANETs (Al-Shareeda et al.
2021a,b), offering valuable insights for designing trustwor-
thy client admission mechanisms in federated learning. To
address the complexity of key management, ECA-VFog
(Almazroi et al. 2023) and CM-CPPA (Al-Shareeda et al.
2022a) introduced efﬁcient authentication protocols based on
certiﬁcateless cryptography and chaotic maps, respectively.
These protocols not only enhance communication security
but also signiﬁcantly reduce computational and communi-
cation costs, making them suitable for resource-constrained
edge devices. At the data-sharing level, Al-Shareeda et al.
(2022b) proposed an efﬁcient scheme that operates with-
out relying on roadside units (RSUs), enabling collaborative
model training in dynamic, distributed environments. Col-
lectively, these studies provide both theoretical foundations
and technical solutions for integrating identity authentica-
tion, privacy protection, and traceable communication into
federated learning systems, helping to mitigate the threat of
model poisoning attacks from the source and improving the
overall robustness and deployability of federated learning
frameworks.
To enhance the defense capabilities of federated learn-
ing systems against security threats such as data poisoning
and model backdoor attacks, a series of research efforts in
image security and steganalysis offer valuable transferable
techniques. Aljarf et al. (2023) leveraged machine learning
and feature extraction for effective color image steganalysis
classiﬁcation, providing insights for anomaly detection and
local model veriﬁcation in image-based federated learning
tasks. Hemalatha et al. (2023) further improved the perfor-
mance of blind steganalyzers by incorporating third-order
SPAM features and ensemble classiﬁers, which could help
identify potential backdoor patterns in client models. The
practicality analysis of feature-based blind steganalysis by
Aljarf et al. (2024) also offers theoretical support for auditing
local models in federated settings. In the domain of image
encryption, Saeidi et al. (2024) integrated Integer Wavelet
Transform(IWT)andHammingcodeswithinasecretsharing
scheme to enhance image conﬁdentiality, which is applicable
to encrypted storage and transmission of private image data
in distributed learning. Gutub’s related works (Gutub 2023;
Gutub and Al-Roithy 2021) proposed dynamic smart prefer-
ences and improved PRNG mechanisms to strengthen image
cryptography and data hiding, offering feasible solutions
for secure and lightweight communication in resource-
constrained federated learning scenarios. Moreover, Singh
et al. (2022) explored AI-based mobile edge computing for
IoT applications, laying a foundation for secure deployment
of federated learning in edge environments. Other contribu-
tions, such as the work by Hassan and Gutub (Hassan and
Gutub 2022) on improving data hiding through the hue com-
ponent of the HSV color space, and by Al-Roithy and Gutub
(Al-Roithy and Gutub 2020) on incorporating chaotic grav-
itational search in PRNG selection, provide theoretical and
algorithmic support for constructing more covert and robust
federated learning defense mechanisms. Collectively, these
studies contribute multi-dimensional insights—from feature
security and image encryption to pseudorandom generation
and communication privacy—that inform the development
of secure and resilient federated learning frameworks.
Recent research has introduced advanced defense mech-
anisms. Nguyen et al. (2022) designed FLAME, which uses
feature space analysis and dynamic weight allocation to
mitigate malicious updates. Sun et al. (2021) developed FL-
WBC, based on weak backdoor authentication, analyzing the
global model and client updates to detect potential back-
door threats. Cao et al. (2021) proposed a provably secure
federated learning method against malicious client attacks,
using robust aggregation and reputation scoring systems.
Jia et al. (2021) introduced a learning proof mechanism
to verify whether models are trained from speciﬁed data
and processes. Wang et al. (2023) enhanced Krum with
a dynamic threshold strategy to improve defense against
backdoor attacks. Zhang et al. (2023) designed a statistical
method to detect malicious updates by analyzing gradient
distributions, magnitudes, and directions, combining robust
aggregationmethodslikeKrumandTrimmedMean.FedTrim
optimizes federated learning aggregation by reducing the
impact of client updates with small norms, minimizing the

based on statistical properties or feature space. This approach
signiﬁcantly reduces the visibility of backdoors in the global
model while enhancing attack robustness and stealth.
3 Threat model
During the entire training process, the attacker does not need
to know the training datasets of all clients. They only need
to know their own poisoned subset and the training param-
eters of their local model. In a federated learning system,
the attacker disguises as a benign client and knows all the
hyperparameter settings of the local training process.
Attacker Capability: Suppose the set of clients participat-
ing in federated learning is C, and the number of clients
is n. Each client can be denoted as Ci(i = 1, 2, 3, ..., n).
The training dataset is D = (x, y), and the dataset of each
client after division is Di(i = 1, 2, 3, ..., n). The attacker
can only control one client C p(1 ≤p ≤n) to launch a
backdoor attack, and the target label is t. Also, the attacker
has the following capabilities: The attacker has the permis-
sion to access and modify the training dataset Dp of the
malicious client C p, and divide Dp into two datasets Dp,1
and Dp,2 according to the poisoned ratio r. The attacker can
create a trigger σ and implant the trigger into the training
dataset Dp,1 to turn x into xσ. Moreover, the corresponding
label y can be modiﬁed to yt, generating the poisoned dataset

Attack goal: By injecting poisoned data, the following
objectives should be achieved: First, malicious updates from

method is proposed. Its invisibility relies on the sparsity
and invisibility constraints applied to the trigger, while its
high attack success rate depends on perturbing speciﬁc pix-
els using gradient values.

5 Experiments
5.1 Experimental setup
5.1.1 Datasets
In the experiment, the CIFAR-10 dataset and PathMNIST
dataset is used. The CIFAR-10 dataset is widely used in
researchonbackdoorattacksinfederatedlearning.PathMNIST
are part of the MedMNIST dataset. PathMNIST consists of
histopathological images derived from colorectal cancer tis-
sue slides. The class distributions of both datasets are shown
in the Table 1.
5.1.2 Poisoning setup
In the trigger generation process, the following parameters
were set: the number of trigger optimization iterations was
200; the number of disturbed pixels representing the sparsity
constraint (k) was set to 150; the perturbation value (eps) was
set to 8; and the perturbation range representing the ampli-
tude constraint was limited to 8/255. The mask update period
(epoch_step) was set to 5, and the perturbation update step
decay (step_decay) was set to 0.8. The target label was set
to 0. Before training, a compromised client was selected, and
federated learning experiments were conducted with poison-
ing rates of 0.01, 0.05, and 0.1.
5.1.3 Training setup
Experiments were conducted on a device equipped with an
RTX 3060 GPU using PyTorch 1.8.1 and CUDA 10.1. A hor-
izontal federated learning strategy was adopted, utilizing a
non-iid data distribution to ensure that each client is assigned
distinct data features. The ResNet18 neural network served
as the base model for federated learning training. Ten clients
were conﬁgured, with a participation ratio of 0.5, meaning
that ﬁve clients were randomly selected from the ten to par-
ticipate in each iteration. For each client, the local training
epochs were set to 5, the batch size for data loading was set
to 10, the learning rate was set to 0.05, and the global training
epochs were set to 1000.
5.1.4 Evaluation metrics
Following previous research on backdoor attacks in feder-
ated learning, we used attack success rate (ASR) as the
primary evaluation metrics (Sun et al. 2021). ASR represents
the classiﬁcation accuracy of the trained global poisoned
model on poisoned test data, indicating the model’s attack
capability.Additionally, two commonly used image quality

5.2.1 Main evaluation

5.2.2 Invisibility
This paper introduces two widely employed image quality
assessment metrics to quantify the changes in image quality
before and after poisoning, thereby reﬂecting the similarity
between the poisoned and original images. The Peak Signal-
to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) is utilized to measure the distortion
level introduced by perturbations added to the image. It quan-
tiﬁes the error between the original and poisoned images
based on pixel value comparisons. Higher PSNR values indi-
cate better image quality and lower distortion. Structural
Similarity Index (SSIM) measures the similarity in terms
of human visual perception following the addition of per-
turbations. SSIM takes into account the image’s brightness,
contrast, and structure, providing a more accurate reﬂection
of image quality that aligns closely with human subjective
experience.Subtractive Pixel Adjacency Matrix (SPAM) and
Spatial Rich Model (SRM) are representative steganalysis
methods that have demonstrated excellent performance in
detecting spatial domain steganographic algorithms. These
techniques are used to identify anomalous patterns in images
that appear normal but have actually been tampered with or
embedded with hidden information.Speciﬁcally, the L1 dif-
ference range of SPAM features between images is 0 to 2.
When the value falls between 0 and 0.3, it indicates that the
SPAM features of the two images are nearly identical. For
SRM features, an L2 difference within the range of 0 to 5
suggests that the poisoned image is very similar to the clean
image.

5.2.4 Ablation experiment
To comprehensively evaluate each module in the proposed
method, ablation studies were designed. Experiments were
conducted under varying poisoning rates and for different
values of L0 and L∞, while all other parameters were main-
tained consistent with those speciﬁed in Section 5.1.3.
1. The impact of different poisoning rates: Experiments
were conducted using poisoning rates of 0.01, 0.05,
0.1, 0.5, and 1. The experimental results are presented
in Fig. 5. Across all schemes, the attack success rate
increased progressively with the increase in poison-
ing budget. Speciﬁcally, when employing the sparse-
invisible scheme and the poisoning budget exceeded
0.1, the attack success rate surpassed 90% for all cases.
In addition, the PSNR and SSIM values reported in
the respective tables indicate that the invisible module
consistently achieved higher performance metrics, with
PSNR values exceeding 35 and SSIM values remaining
above 0.9.
2. The impact of different L∞: Experiments were con-
ducted under the constraints of eps set to 2, 4, 6, 8,
and 10. The experimental results are presented in Fig. 6.
It was observed that the attack success rate increased
progressively with higher values of eps. Notably, when
employing the sparse scheme with eps > 6, the attack
success rate consistently exceeded 90% across all cases,
whereas other schemes exhibited relatively lower success
rates. In terms of PSNR and SSIM metrics, the invisible
module demonstrated consistently superior performance.
Speciﬁcally, the PSNR values for the invisible scheme
were uniformly greater than 35, and the SSIM values
exceeded 0.9.
3. The impact of different L0: Experiments were conducted
under the constraints of k set to 50, 100, 150, 200, and
250. The experimental results are presented in Fig. 7.
It was observed that the attack success rate increased
progressively with higher values of k. Notably, when
employing the sparse scheme with k > 150, the attack
success rate consistently exceeded 90% across all cases,
whereas other schemes exhibited relatively lower success
rates. In terms of PSNR and SSIM metrics, the invisible
module demonstrated consistently superior performance.
Speciﬁcally, the PSNR values for the invisible scheme
were uniformly greater than 30, and the SSIM values
exceeded 0.9.

module signiﬁcantly inﬂuences the attack success rate of the
trigger, while the invisible module substantially impacts the
trigger’s invisibility. Compared to alternative schemes, the
proposed sparse-invisible scheme in this paper achieves both
a high attack success rate and superior invisibility,it can be
observed that when the poisoning rate > 0.05, eps ≥6, and
k ≥100,the ASR remains stable.

Abstract: In distributed edge Computing scenarios within the Internet of Things (IoT), individual clients are susceptible to adversarial backdoor attacks, wherein malicious modiﬁcations to local data may be introduced. Such compromised clients can negatively impact the integrity and performance of the global model during federated learning. Existing backdoor attack techniques suffer from low attack success rates and poor trigger concealment. To address this issue, this paper proposes a novel Sparse and Invisible Targeted Backdoor (SITB) attack method. The key advantages of SITB are as follows: (1) A sparse and invisible trigger generation approach is introduced, enforcing sparsity and invisibility constraints during optimization to enhance trigger concealment. (2) In sparse constraints, by ranking gradient values and selecting pixels most sensitive to the model, the method achieves a high attack success rate. Extensive experiments on the CIFAR-10 public dataset and PathMNIST dataset validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. Results show that the attack success rate on poisoned data surpasses existing methods by 5–10%. Furthermore, the quantitative assessment of visual quality, conducted both prior to and subsequent to poisoning, afﬁrmed that the generated trigger exhibited a high degree of stealthiness, boasting a PSNR value as high as 40 and an SSIM value as high as 0.99. In addition, SPAM and SRM are extremely low. Moreover, it demonstrates robust resistance against multiple federated learning defense mechanisms.
